sections.heading: Roots: Article 40, State List and the idea of decentralisation

blocks.title: Constitutional base
head: Provision
What it says
rows: Article 40 (Part IV – Directive Principles of State Policy)
'The State shall take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government.'
'Local government' is a State subject – not Union List, not Concurrent List. So each state makes its own Panchayati Raj law.
Gave practical shape to Article 40 and gave panchayats constitutional status (details on the 73rd Amendment card).

blocks.title: Key ideas
head: Term
Meaning
rows: Management of local affairs by locally elected persons (not by officials appointed by the government).
The system of rural local self-government; its institutions are institutions of self-government.
Transferring real powers, functions and resources to elected local bodies answerable to local people. Local self-government is best explained as an exercise in democratic decentralisation.
Only shifting administrative work to field offices of the same government; no decision power passes to elected bodies.
Transfer of decision-making to semi-autonomous bodies that stay accountable to the government.
Transfer of power to autonomous, elected local governments.
Transfer of functions to the private or voluntary sector.

A function should go to the lowest level of government that can do it well. Example: a tank that serves only one village should be managed by that village's gram panchayat. Higher levels still have a role – they are not shut out.
Latin for 'empire within an empire', meaning a government within the government. It is used for local bodies, which work like small governments inside the State.
People take part directly in decisions, as in the Gram Sabha.
Decisions are taken through elected representatives.
Giving taxes, fees and grants to local bodies.

blocks.title: Centralised vs decentralised system
head: Aspect
Centralised
Decentralised
rows: Spread among many levels, including local bodies
Higher – people and local bodies take part
Uses local knowledge and resources; trains citizens in democracy; reduces workload of higher governments; makes leaders accountable because they are close to the people
blocks.note: In India's parliamentary system, power gets centralised to some extent at the Prime Minister or Chief Minister level, and a charismatic leader increases this. People do not take policy decisions directly.

blocks.title: Fundamental object of Panchayati Raj (UPSC 2015)
head: Included
Not the answer

sections.heading: Before Panchayati Raj: rural experiments, CDP (1952) and NES (1953)

blocks.title: Rural reconstruction experiments before 1952
head: Experiment (year)
Place
Led by

Spencer Hatch, American agricultural expert, with help of the YMCA
Albert Mayer (American); forerunner and model for the CDP
S.K. Dey; for rehabilitation of Partition refugees
blocks.note: Chronological order: Gurgaon (1920), then Marthandam (1921), then Baroda (1932), then Firka (1946), then Etawah (1948). Etawah was led by Albert Mayer; only Nilokheri was led by S.K. Dey.

blocks.title: Community Development Programme (CDP) and National Extension Service (NES)
head: Point
Fact
rows: Grow More Food Enquiry Committee (1952) under V.T. Krishnamachari – urged an integrated rural programme
Ford Foundation (USA) – financial and technical support
S.K. Dey – called a 'social engineer'; first Union Minister for Community Development and Cooperation

Community welfare through the development of each individual; people's participation in all-round development; and an attack on poverty, unemployment and illiteracy, using local resources with help from government and voluntary bodies. It covered agriculture, health, education and infrastructure.
Development block (usually about 100 villages) under a Block Development Officer (BDO)
Village Level Worker (Gram Sevak) – multipurpose extension worker for a group of villages
Supervising offices at Centre, State (Development Commissioner), District (Collector) and Block (BDO). No elected zila parishads in 1952.
2 October 1953 – one year AFTER the CDP, as a supplement to it (it did not replace the CDP)
To give technical help and to put unused ('dormant') rural manpower to work
Programme Evaluation Organisation set up in 1952 to evaluate the CDP
It was run from the top by officials, and villagers were treated as receivers, not partners. So it failed to get people's participation.

sections.heading: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) and the first states

blocks.title: Basic facts
head: Point
Fact
rows: January 1957, by the Government of India (through the Committee on Plan Projects); Jawaharlal Nehru was Prime Minister
To examine the working of the CDP (1952) and NES (1953) and suggest better working. It was NOT about the 73rd Amendment (which came 35 years later).
'Democratic decentralisation' – later called Panchayati Raj. This committee was the first to use this term. The present pattern of panchayats owes its parentage (origin) to this committee.
It found the CDP and NES had failed to get people's participation.

blocks.title: Recommendations
head: Topic
Recommendation
rows: Three-tier: gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block), zila parishad (district)
The three tiers were to be 'organically linked' (joined into one chain) through indirect elections
Gram panchayat – directly elected. Panchayat samiti and zila parishad – indirectly elected.
Panchayat samiti (block level) – the executive body and the basic unit
Only an advisory, coordinating and supervisory body (not the executive body)
All planning and development work should be given to these bodies, with a genuine transfer of power and responsibility
Adequate resources should be transferred to these bodies. It did NOT recommend a power to levy income tax.
A system should be built to transfer (devolve) still more authority to these bodies in future
It did NOT recommend: constitutional recognition, official participation of political parties, a two-tier system, direct election of the zila parishad, or any formal mention of the Gram Sabha

blocks.title: National Development Council response (Jan 1958)
head: Point
Fact
rows: It did not insist on a single rigid pattern – states were free to develop their own patterns suited to local conditions
However, the basic principles and broad fundamentals must be the same across the country

blocks.title: First states
head: Order
State
Detail
rows: Inaugurated by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on 2 October 1959 in Nagaur district. Rajasthan was also the first state where Panchayati Raj was implemented in the whole state.
Also in 1959; the first panchayat in Andhra Pradesh was formed at Shadnagar (then Mahabubnagar district, now in Telangana) on 11 October 1959
blocks.note: Most states set up Panchayati Raj by the mid-1960s.

blocks.title: Early state patterns
head: State or pattern
Feature
rows: The panchayat samiti was the powerful body, because the block was the unit of planning
The zila parishad was the powerful body, because the district was the unit of planning
Judicial panchayats in some states to try petty civil and criminal cases

blocks.title: Basic facts
head: Point
Fact
rows: December 1977, by the Janata Government; Morarji Desai was Prime Minister
Panchayati Raj on the Balwant Rai Mehta model had declined and had not given the expected results
Janata Government fell before completing its term, so no action at the Centre. Karnataka, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh revitalised Panchayati Raj using it (not Rajasthan).

blocks.title: Recommendations
head: Topic
Recommendation
rows: Two tiers: zila parishad (district level) and, below it, the mandal panchayat; a term of four years
A group of villages with a total population of 15,000 to 20,000; it is the lowest elected tier, below the zila parishad
The district should be the first level below the state where power is decentralised, under the supervision of the people's elected representatives
The zila parishad, responsible for planning at district level. All development functions and staff to work under it (not under the Collector).
Political parties should officially take part at all levels of panchayat elections
Panchayats should have compulsory powers of taxation to raise their own money
By a district-level agency and a committee of legislators – to check that funds for weaker sections are actually spent on them
The state should not supersede (dissolve) Panchayati Raj institutions (PRIs). If it must, fresh elections should be held within six months.
Nyaya (judicial) panchayats should be kept separate from development panchayats and be presided over by a qualified judge
Chief Electoral Officer of the state, in consultation with the Chief Election Commissioner
Voluntary agencies should help mobilise people's support for Panchayati Raj
A minister for Panchayati Raj in the state council of ministers
Seats reserved for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in proportion to their population
Constitutional recognition for PRIs – it was the first committee to recommend this

blocks.title: Balwant Rai Mehta vs Ashok Mehta
head: Aspect
Balwant Rai Mehta (1957)
Ashok Mehta (1977)
rows: Advisory, coordinating and supervisory only; the Collector is its chairman
Executive and planning body; development staff under it
Entrust planning and development work to elected local bodies

blocks.title: Study teams 1960–1976 (Laxmikanth Table 39.1)
head: Year
Study team or committee
Chairman
rows: Working Group on Panchayats and Cooperatives
Study Team on Panchayati Raj Administration
Position of Gram Sabha in Panchayati Raj Movement
Budgeting and Accounting Procedure of PRIs
Audit and Accounts of Panchayati Raj Bodies

Committee on Community Development and Panchayati Raj

blocks.title: Planning committees and later committees
head: Committee (year)
Set up on
Key recommendation
rows: Block as the unit of planning
Separate district planning bodies, headed by either the Collector or a minister; the Collector should coordinate all development work in the district
Set up by the Planning Commission on existing administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation

Development work had become bureaucratised (run by officials), leaving PRIs like 'grass without roots'. The district (not the block) is the proper unit for planning, and the zila parishad should be the central body. A new post of District Development Commissioner should act as chief executive of the zila parishad. Elections should be held regularly – they were overdue in 11 states.
Rajiv Gandhi Government; 'Revitalisation of PRIs for Democracy and Development'

Constitutional recognition by adding a new chapter to the Constitution; regular, free and fair elections; nyaya panchayats for a cluster of villages; villages reorganised so that gram panchayats are viable (able to work); Gram Sabha called the 'embodiment of direct democracy'; more money for village panchayats; judicial tribunals in each state to settle disputes about panchayat elections and dissolution
A sub-committee of a Consultative Committee of Parliament; it examined the political and administrative structure of the district for district planning

Constitutional recognition; three tiers; zila parishad as the pivot (central body); fixed five-year term; a body can be superseded for at most six months; a list of panchayat subjects in the Constitution; reservation of seats by population and also for women; a State Finance Commission; the Collector as chief executive officer of the zila parishad
The Congress party's Committee on Policy and Programmes; it was asked 'how best PRIs could be made effective'

Constitutional status; three tiers; five-year term; direct election at all three levels; reservation for SCs, STs and women; a list of subjects in the Constitution; power to levy taxes; a State Finance Commission; a State Election Commission. Its recommendations became the basis of the constitutional amendment bill.
blocks.note: Balwant Rai Mehta, the First Administrative Reforms Commission, Ashok Mehta and G.V.K. Rao all wanted the Collector to have a SMALLER role in development; only Hanumantha Rao wanted the Collector to coordinate it.

head: Committee
Subject

items.what: 64th Amendment Bill (Rajiv Gandhi Government) introduced in Lok Sabha
items.detail: The Lok Sabha passed it in August 1989, but the Rajya Sabha did not approve it, so it failed. The Opposition said it would strengthen centralisation.

items.what: V.P. Singh Government introduced a fresh bill
items.detail: It lapsed when the government fell.

items.what: P.V. Narasimha Rao Government introduced a modified bill

items.what: 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act passed
items.detail: Added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects). Details are on the 73rd Amendment card.

items.what: 73rd Amendment came into force
items.detail: So 24 April is National Panchayati Raj Day.

items.what: 74th Amendment (municipalities) came into force

blocks.text: see 73rd Amendment card for its provisions

items: 'Local government' is in the State List (Entry 5) – not the Concurrent List. Article 40 is a Directive Principle in Part IV.
CDP (2 October 1952) came BEFORE NES (2 October 1953). The CDP was not set up on Balwant Rai Mehta's advice – that committee came later (1957) to review it.
Rajasthan was first (Nagaur, 2 October 1959); Andhra Pradesh was second (Shadnagar, 1959) – Andhra Pradesh did not start in 1958.
Balwant Rai Mehta: three tiers; the panchayat samiti is the executive body; the Collector chairs the zila parishad; no official role for political parties; no constitutional status.

Ashok Mehta: two tiers, zila parishad is the executive body, political parties allowed officially, compulsory taxation powers, elections within six months after supersession (dissolution). It was the FIRST committee to recommend constitutional recognition (1978). L.M. Singhvi (1986) came later and asked for a new chapter in the Constitution – so a key saying 'Singhvi first suggested constitutional status' is wrong by Laxmikanth.
'Grass without roots' = G.V.K. Rao. Gram Sabha as 'embodiment of direct democracy' = L.M. Singhvi.
Order of committees: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957), then Dantwala (1978), then Hanumantha Rao (1984), then G.V.K. Rao (1985), then L.M. Singhvi (1986), then Thungon and Gadgil (both 1988).
The 64th Amendment Bill (1989) passed the Lok Sabha but failed in the Rajya Sabha. Decentralisation helps SCs, STs and women – but calling them 'minorities' is wrong.

subcards.title: 73rd Amendment: Part IX (Art 243–243O) & Eleventh Schedule
subcards.summary: How the Constitution sets up panchayats: tiers, elections, reservation, money and PESA.
at_a_glance: 73rd Amendment, 1992; came into force on 24 April 1993
Part IX (Art 243 to Art 243-O, 16 articles) and the Eleventh Schedule
Three levels: village, intermediate (block) and district. A state with population up to 20 lakh may skip the intermediate level
Not less than one-third of seats and chairpersons
Five years; if dissolved early, a fresh election within six months
State Election Commission (Art 243K), State Finance Commission (Art 243-I)
Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Scheduled Areas. The PESA Act, 1996 extends Part IX to Scheduled Areas with changes

blocks.title: The Act in one view
head: Point
Fact
rows: Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992 — it set up panchayats as units of self-government in rural areas
In the Lok Sabha in September 1991 by the P.V. Narasimha Rao government
1992 (the 74th Amendment on municipalities was also passed in 1992)
Needed because 'local government' is a State List subject (Seventh Schedule), so at least half the state legislatures had to approve it. 17 state assemblies approved it
Given by President Shankar Dayal Sharma on 20 April 1993 (not by R. Venkataraman)
24 April 1993 — celebrated as National Panchayati Raj Day
A new Part IX ('The Panchayats', Articles 243 to 243-O, which is 16 articles) and a new Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)
Article 40 — the State shall organise village panchayats as units of self-government

blocks.title: Articles 243 to 243-O at a glance
head: Article
Subject
rows: Definitions (Gram Sabha in clause (b), village, panchayat area)
Powers, authority and responsibilities of panchayats (linked to the Eleventh Schedule)
Powers to impose taxes, and funds of panchayats
Part IX not to apply to certain areas
Continuance of existing laws and panchayats (for one year)
Bar to interference by courts in electoral matters
blocks.note: Do not mix these with Part IXA (municipalities). There, Art 243R is composition of municipalities, Art 243U is their term, Art 243Y is their Finance Commission, Art 243ZA is their elections, and Art 243ZD is the District Planning Committee.

blocks.title: Four dimensions of decentralisation and their Articles
head: Dimension
Provision
rows: Art 243K (State Election Commission), direct election to all seats, and a fixed five-year term
Art 243-I (State Finance Commission), along with Art 243H (taxes and grants)

blocks.text: For Part IXA, the District Planning Committee and the Metropolitan Planning Committee, see the card '74th Amendment: Municipalities'

blocks.title: Why it matters
items: It gave panchayats constitutional status. Before 1992 they existed only under state laws.

It put panchayats in the justiciable part of the Constitution (the part that courts can enforce). So states are now bound to set up panchayats and hold regular elections; this no longer depends on the state government's wish.
It made the panchayat structure uniform across India (three tiers in every state).
Laxmikanth: it changes representative democracy (people decide through elected members) into participatory democracy (people decide directly, as in the Gram Sabha).
Panchayats are institutions of self-government. The idea is democratic decentralisation: power moves down to elected local bodies.
Subsidiarity (a decision should be taken at the lowest level able to take it) is reflected in devolving planning and development to panchayats (Art 243G).
Imperium in imperio (Latin) means 'a government within the government' — a phrase used for a local body that works as a government of its own inside the state.
Fiscal decentralisation means giving local bodies their own taxes, fees and grants (money matters, not just duties).

blocks.title: Gram Sabha — the base of the system
head: Point
Fact
rows: Article 243(b): all persons registered in the electoral rolls (voters' list) of a village within the panchayat area
Article 243A — the Gram Sabha may exercise the powers and functions that the state legislature decides
Having a Gram Sabha is compulsory. Giving it powers is voluntary (left to the state). Its powers are NOT listed in the Eleventh Schedule (that Schedule lists subjects for panchayats)
It is an example of direct democracy; often called the 'soul' of Panchayati Raj
An area the Governor specifies as a village by public notification (Article 243)

blocks.text: For committees before 1992 (Balwant Rai Mehta, Ashok Mehta, L.M. Singhvi, Thungon, Gadgil) and the failed 64th Amendment Bill, see the card 'Panchayati Raj: evolution and committees'

blocks.title: Structure and elections
head: Topic
Rule
rows: Village, intermediate (block) and district levels in every state
A state whose population is not more than 20 lakh may skip the intermediate (block) tier. So intermediate panchayats do not exist in every state
All seats at all three levels are filled by direct election by the people
As far as practicable, the ratio of a panchayat area's population to its number of seats is the same throughout the state

Chairpersons of intermediate and district panchayats are elected indirectly, by the elected members from among themselves. The village chairperson (sarpanch) is elected in the way the state legislature decides
Chairpersons and all members, whether elected directly or indirectly, can vote in panchayat meetings
The state may give them seats in intermediate or district panchayats. Rajya Sabha MPs and Legislative Council members (MLCs) can get a seat in the panchayat area where they are registered as voters

blocks.title: Reservation (Art 243D)
head: Group
Rule
rows: Compulsory. Seats are reserved at all three levels, in proportion to their share of the population in the panchayat area. Chairperson posts are also reserved
Compulsory. Not less than one-third of total seats, and this one-third INCLUDES the seats for SC and ST women. Also not less than one-third of chairperson posts at each level
Not less than one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs go to women of those groups
Seats reserved for women are allotted by rotation to different constituencies
Voluntary. The state legislature MAY reserve seats and chairperson posts for them (Art 243D(6))

SC and ST reservation in panchayats ends when the period in Article 334 ends — now 2030 (extended by the 104th Amendment, 2019). Women's reservation is NOT tied to Article 334, so it does not end in 2030
Its panchayats have no SC reservation, because it has no Scheduled Castes. This was added as Art 243M(3A) by the 83rd Amendment, 2000

blocks.title: 50% reservation for women (as of Nov 2026)
items: The Constitution says 'not less than one-third'. So a state law giving 50% to women is valid — one-third is only the minimum.
Union government reply in the Lok Sabha (16 December 2025): 21 states and 2 Union Territories give 50% reservation to women in panchayats.

States: Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Tripura, Uttarakhand, West Bengal.
Union Territories: Lakshadweep; Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
Bihar was the first state to give 50% (2006). The constitutional minimum is one-third, so an option saying '30%' is wrong.

blocks.title: Case on backward-class reservation
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Upheld Art 243D(6) and Art 243T(6), which allow backward-class reservation in panchayats and municipalities; they do not violate the basic structure. Also upheld reserving chairperson posts (Art 243D(4) and Art 243T(4))

The Court said local-body reservation is a separate basis, different from reservation in education and jobs under Art 15(4) and Art 16(4), so those tests cannot simply be applied. States must first collect data on backwardness, and total vertical reservation (SC, ST and backward classes together) should not cross 50%, except to protect STs in Scheduled Areas. The 'triple test' was later laid down on this basis in Vikas Kishanrao Gawali (2021)

blocks.title: Term (Art 243E) and disqualification (Art 243F)
head: Topic
Rule
rows: Five years, counted from the date fixed for its first meeting, at every level. It can be dissolved before that
Must be completed before the five-year term ends
Must be completed within six months of dissolution
If less than six months of the term was left at dissolution, no election is needed for that short period
Serves only the rest of the old body's term, not a fresh five years
First meeting 1 July 2022, dissolved 1 July 2025. So the election must be held by 1 January 2026, and the new body serves only till 30 June 2027 (the end of the old term)
21 years. Art 243F says nobody is disqualified for being under 25 if he or she has reached 21. The same 21 applies at every tier — not 25, not 30
Any ground that disqualifies a person under the law for state legislature elections, or any ground in a law made by the state legislature
An authority that the state legislature provides by law
NOT in the Constitution. (The rule bars people with more than two children from contesting.) Some states put it in their own laws, so a state can also remove it by amending its law

blocks.text: For sarpanch elections, Gram Sabha meetings and backward-class (BC) reservation in Andhra Pradesh, and the 2026 polls, see the card 'Panchayati Raj in Andhra Pradesh'

blocks.title: Laxmikanth's list
head: Aspect
Compulsory (state law must have it)
Voluntary (state may choose)
rows: Organise a Gram Sabha in a village or group of villages
Give the Gram Sabha powers and functions
Panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels
Direct election to all seats; indirect election of chairpersons of intermediate and district panchayats
Manner of electing the village chairperson
Voting right of chairpersons and members
Seats for village chairpersons in intermediate (or district) panchayats; for intermediate chairpersons in district panchayats; and for MPs and MLAs (of both Houses) in panchayats
For SCs and STs (seats and chairperson posts); one-third for women (seats and chairperson posts)
Five-year term; fresh election within six months of dissolution
State Election Commission; State Finance Commission every five years
Giving panchayats powers to work as self-government; giving them the job of making plans, and some or all of the 29 Eleventh Schedule subjects
Power to levy taxes, tolls and fees; handing over some state taxes; grants-in-aid; setting up panchayat funds

blocks.title: Watch out
items: Audit of accounts (Art 243J) is NOT in the compulsory list — the state legislature 'may' provide for it.
Representation of MPs and MLAs is voluntary.
The Act did not provide regular salary or remuneration for panchayat members.
Panchayats cannot make laws. Only the state legislature can give them taxing powers.

sections.heading: Election Commission, Finance Commission and money

blocks.title: State Election Commission (Art 243K)
head: Point
Fact
rows: Superintendence, direction and control (full charge) of preparing voters' lists and of all panchayat elections — for example it issues election notifications and allots symbols
The Governor, who also fixes conditions of service and tenure
Only in the same way and on the same grounds as a High Court judge — not by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister or ministers
Service conditions cannot be changed to his or her disadvantage after appointment
The same State Election Commission conducts municipal elections (Art 243ZA)
The Election Commission of India (ECI, Art 324) conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President — not to panchayats or municipalities
Constitutional status came by the 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992

An Election Commissioner of the ECI (not the Chief Election Commissioner) is less protected from removal than a State Election Commissioner. He or she can be removed on the Chief Election Commissioner's recommendation, while a State Election Commissioner can be removed only like a High Court judge

blocks.title: State Finance Commission (Art 243-I)
head: Point
Fact
rows: The Governor (acting for the state government) sets it up every five years — not the President, not the Chief Minister
How the net money from state taxes, duties, tolls and fees should be shared between the state and panchayats, and then among the panchayats
Which taxes, duties, tolls and fees may be assigned to panchayats
Grants-in-aid to panchayats from the state's Consolidated Fund
Steps to improve panchayat finances, and any other matter the Governor refers to it
Fixed by the state legislature by law — not by the Constitution
The Governor places it, with an action-taken memorandum, before the state legislature
Auditing panchayat accounts; sharing Union taxes among states (that is the job of the Union Finance Commission)
Art 243Y (in Part IXA) uses the same State Finance Commission for municipalities

blocks.title: Link with the Union Finance Commission (Art 280)
head: Point
Fact
rows: Suggest steps to increase a state's Consolidated Fund so that the state can give more money to its panchayats
The recommendations of that state's Finance Commission
The 73rd Amendment added Art 280(3)(bb) for panchayats; the 74th Amendment added Art 280(3)(c) for municipalities. This duty was not in the original 1950 Constitution
Grants to gram panchayats split as 90% basic grant (given without conditions) and 10% performance grant (given only on meeting set conditions) — ratio 90:10

Total grants about Rs 9.47 lakh crore. Of this, about 83.5% (Rs 7.91 lakh crore) is for rural and urban local bodies — the largest share. Rural local bodies get Rs 4.35 lakh crore. For both rural and urban bodies, 80% is basic grant and 20% is performance grant (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Finances (Art 243H) and sources of money
head: Point
Fact
rows: (a) let panchayats levy, collect and keep taxes, duties, tolls and fees; (b) assign state-collected taxes to them; (c) give grants-in-aid from the state's Consolidated Fund; (d) create funds for panchayat money

Union grants on the advice of the Central (Union) Finance Commission; money passed on by the state on the advice of the State Finance Commission; loans or grants from the state; money from Centrally Sponsored Schemes; and the panchayat's own taxes and non-tax income
Panchayats have responsibility but grossly inadequate resources; they depend heavily on grants, even in Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu
Gram panchayats have their own taxes (property or house tax, profession tax, water and street-light charges, and so on). Intermediate and district tiers depend on tolls, fees and non-tax income
Audit of accounts is under Art 243J. Social audit (people checking how the money was spent) by a district-level agency was recommended by the Ashok Mehta Committee

sections.heading: Exempted areas, Union Territories and PESA

blocks.title: Where Part IX applies
head: Article
Rule
rows: Applies to Union Territories; the President may direct exceptions and modifications
Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram (they have their own traditional councils)
Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under Art 244; hill areas of Manipur that have district councils; and Darjeeling district of West Bengal, which has the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council
Parliament may by law extend Part IX to Scheduled and tribal areas with changes. It did this through the PESA Act, 1996
No SC reservation in Arunachal Pradesh (83rd Amendment, 2000)

Old state laws that clashed with Part IX could continue for at most one year from 24 April 1993. So most states passed new Acts in 1993–94 (for example, the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act, 1994). Panchayats already in office could finish their term

No court can question laws on delimitation (drawing boundaries) of constituencies or on allotment of seats. A panchayat election can be challenged only by an election petition before the authority named in state law — not by a writ petition first. Art 329 is the similar bar for Parliament and state legislature elections
blocks.note: Part IX applies to states like Odisha and Arunachal Pradesh. Older answer keys (before 2019) also list Jammu and Kashmir as outside Part IX, because of its special status then. Since 2019 Jammu and Kashmir is a Union Territory and Part IX applies there.

blocks.title: PESA Act, 1996 (Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act)
head: Point
Fact
rows: It extends Part IX, with changes, to Fifth Schedule (Scheduled) Areas, so that tribal people can govern themselves
Ten states with Fifth Schedule Areas
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan (Assam is NOT one — it has Sixth Schedule areas)
Made up of all voters of the village. It protects tribal customs, cultural identity, community resources and the traditional way of settling disputes
Plans and projects, before the village panchayat carries them out. It also picks the beneficiaries of poverty-removal schemes
The village panchayat must get a certificate from the Gram Sabha that the funds were used properly
Scheduled Tribes: not less than one-half of seats. ALL chairperson posts at all levels reserved for Scheduled Tribes
The state may nominate STs who have no representation to intermediate or district panchayats — at most one-tenth (not one-third) of the number of elected members
The Gram Sabha or panchayat must be consulted before land is acquired and before people are resettled
For minor minerals, the recommendation of the Gram Sabha or panchayat is compulsory before a prospecting licence or mining lease is given, and before auctions

Enforce prohibition or control the sale of intoxicants; own minor forest produce; stop land alienation (tribal land passing to outsiders) and restore tribal land taken illegally; manage village markets; control money-lending to STs; control social-sector institutions and their staff; control local plans, including tribal sub-plans
Administration at district level should follow the Sixth Schedule pattern (autonomous councils)
Gram Sabhas cannot declare an area a Scheduled Area (only the President can). PESA also does not create autonomous regions
Notified its PESA Rules only in January 2026 (state cabinet approved them on 23 December 2025), about 25 years after Jharkhand was formed (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: The 29 subjects (linked to Art 243G)
head: No.
Subject
rows: Land improvement, land reforms, land consolidation and soil conservation
Minor irrigation, water management and watershed development
Rural electrification, including distribution of electricity
Education, including primary and secondary schools
Health and sanitation, including hospitals, primary health centres and dispensaries
Social welfare, including welfare of the handicapped and mentally retarded
Welfare of weaker sections, especially SCs and STs
blocks.note: NOT in the Eleventh Schedule: fire services, urban planning, slum improvement, cattle pounds and prevention of cruelty to animals (these are in the Twelfth Schedule, for municipalities). Higher education and regulation of land revenue are also not in it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Art 243G does NOT force states to transfer all 29 subjects. It only lets the state legislature give panchayats powers for (a) preparing plans and (b) implementing schemes for economic development and social justice. So panchayat strength varies from state to state.
The Eleventh Schedule has 29 items (for panchayats, added by the 73rd Amendment). The Twelfth Schedule has 18 items (for municipalities, added by the 74th Amendment).
'Local government' is a State List subject — not the Concurrent List.

blocks.title: Schedules added by amendments
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law: disqualification of members who change party)
Special status for Delhi as the National Capital Territory (Art 239AA)
Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (Panchayati Raj)
Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule (municipalities)
Setting up of state-level rent tribunals
Accepted the 10th Finance Commission's 'alternative scheme' of sharing Union taxes with the states
No SC reservation in Arunachal Pradesh panchayats
Right to Education (Art 21A: free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14)
SC and ST reservation in Lok Sabha and state assemblies extended to 2030

blocks.title: Other Schedules and Parts often mixed in
head: Item
Content
rows: Salaries and allowances of high offices, including the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of state assemblies
Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
Part IX is on panchayats; Part IXA is on municipalities (so municipal powers are in Part IXA, not Part IX)
Part XVIII is on Emergency provisions; Part XX is on Amendment of the Constitution

sections.heading: Why panchayats are weak, and state practices

blocks.title: Reasons for ineffective performance (Laxmikanth)
head: Reason
Meaning
rows: States have not handed over the '3Fs' — Functions (work), Funds (money) and Functionaries (staff)
Sarpanches spend much of their time at Block Offices, waiting for funds and technical approval from officials
Scheme money comes 'tied' — it must be spent only on fixed activities, which may not suit every village
Since the money comes from the government and not from the people's own taxes, people rarely demand a social audit (a public check of spending)
Panchayat heads find it hard to tax their own neighbours (for example property tax or street-light charges), so they avoid it
Many state laws do not spell out its powers or procedures
Separate 'Missions' or societies, with more money than the panchayat, do the work and bypass the panchayat
Many panchayats have no full-time secretary or office building, and members are often untrained
blocks.note: These are NOT cited as reasons: 'too many constitutional articles' and 'excessive judicial interference in elections'.

blocks.title: Devolution Index (Ministry of Panchayati Raj)
items: It measures six dimensions: Framework, Functions, Finances, Functionaries, Capacity Building (also called capacity enhancement) and Accountability. Electoral turnout is NOT one of them.
2024 report (released February 2025): the top three states are Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

blocks.title: Good practices in states (G.B.K. notes and state studies, not Laxmikanth)
head: State
Practice
rows: Gives more than one-third (about 35–40%) of state plan funds to panchayats, untied (panchayats decide how to spend it). An independent Ombudsman looks into complaints against panchayat members. The beneficiary list chosen by the Gram Sabha cannot be changed, not even by the Collector. Self-help groups (Kudumbashree neighbourhood groups) are linked to the Gram Sabha. Agriculture and health staff were transferred to panchayats. People can inspect and copy panchayat registers

Three standing committees at village level: Production, Social Justice, and Amenities. 'Jamabandi' (a yearly public audit of panchayat accounts, a practice borrowed from the Revenue Department, started in 2001). All 29 Eleventh Schedule subjects devolved to the Zilla Panchayat
'Operation Barga' — land reform carried out through panchayats. It registered bargadars (sharecroppers who till another person's land). 'Barga' means sharecropping, not a group of tribes
The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Zilla Parishad is an IAS officer. A Mahila Gram Sabha (a meeting of the village's women voters) is held before the general Gram Sabha

Voters have the right to recall (remove before the term ends) the sarpanch and ward members. In Haryana (2020 law): 50% of Gram Sabha or ward members ask in writing, then a secret ballot; the member is removed if two-thirds vote against him or her. The exact steps differ from state to state

items: Women: 'not less than one-third' (about 33%) of seats, including SC and ST women — never '30%'. A state law giving 50% is valid; 21 states and 2 Union Territories give it (as of Nov 2026).
These are all voluntary (left to the state): backward-class reservation, powers of the Gram Sabha, taxing powers, seats for MPs and MLAs in panchayats, and audit of accounts.
Minimum age is 21 at every tier. The intermediate tier is optional only for states with population up to 20 lakh.
After dissolution, a fresh election must be held within six months, and the new body serves only the rest of the old term.
State Election Commissioner: appointed by the Governor, removed only like a High Court judge. The Election Commission of India does not conduct local elections.

State Finance Commission: set up by the Governor every five years; its composition is fixed by state law. The Union Finance Commission suggests help to the state on the basis of its report (Art 280(3)(bb)).

Not covered by Part IX: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas, Manipur hill areas and Darjeeling. Under PESA: at least one-half of seats for STs, all chairpersons must be STs, and nomination of up to one-tenth.
Eleventh Schedule has 29 items (fire services is not one); Twelfth Schedule has 18. The two-child rule comes from state laws, not from the 73rd Amendment.

subcards.title: Panchayati Raj in Andhra Pradesh
subcards.summary: How Andhra Pradesh's village, mandal and district councils grew, how they work and how they are elected.
at_a_glance: Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (in force 30 May 1994)
Gram Panchayat (village), Mandal Praja Parishad (mandal), Zilla Praja Parishad (district)
Shadnagar, 11 October 1959. AP was the 2nd state after Rajasthan.
1986 Act of the N.T. Rama Rao government; Mandal Praja Parishads were first formed on 15 January 1987
State Election Commission (AP after the 2014 division)
28 districts; the 13 Zilla Parishads are being reorganised into 28, one per district (as of Nov 2026)
Local body elections held from October to December 2026 (as of Nov 2026)

sections.heading: Growth of Panchayati Raj in AP: laws and dates

items.what: Madras Local Boards Act
items.detail: Covered the Andhra area while it was part of the Madras Presidency.

items.what: Madras Village Panchayats Act
items.detail: When Andhra State was formed in 1953, this Act governed village panchayats in the Andhra area. It gave a two-tier system.

items.what: Hyderabad Gram Panchayat Act
items.detail: Covered the Telangana area (the old Hyderabad State). So, before 1964, the Andhra and Telangana regions had separate panchayat laws.

items.what: AP Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act
items.detail: Made the system three-tier: village panchayat, Panchayat Samithi at the block level, and Zilla Parishad at the district level.

items.what: Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj in AP at Shadnagar
items.detail: Shadnagar is now in Telangana (Rangareddy district). Rajasthan was first (Nagaur, 2 October 1959); AP was second, in the same year.

items.what: AP Gram Panchayats Act
items.detail: One law for the village panchayats of the whole state (Act 2 of 1964).

items.what: AP Municipalities Act
items.detail: This is an urban (town) law, but exam questions often mix it with the panchayat laws.

items.what: AP Mandal Praja Parishads, Zilla Praja Parishads and Zilla Pranalika Abhivruddhi Sameeksha Mandals Act
items.detail: Act 31 of 1986. The N.T. Rama Rao government replaced the Panchayat Samithis (334 of them, as per AP government training material) with Mandal Praja Parishads.

items.what: Mandal Praja Parishads first formed (new mandal system came into effect)
AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994
items.detail: Brought all three tiers under one law, in line with the 73rd Amendment. It repealed the 1964 Act and the 1986 Act (Section 276).

items.what: AP Panchayat Raj (Amendment) Act, 1998 (Act 7 of 1998) — AP's PESA law
items.detail: PESA means the Central Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996. AP's 1998 Act added special rules for tribal (Fifth Schedule) areas into the 1994 Act (Part VI-A, Sections 242A to 242I).

items.what: AP District Planning Committees Act, 2004 (Act 5 of 2004)
items.detail: Sets up the District Planning Committee required by Art 243ZD. It is treated as in force from 30 December 2003, when an ordinance on it was issued.

items.what: Telangana Panchayat Raj Act
items.detail: Telangana's own law after the 2014 bifurcation (division) of AP.

blocks.title: Why the 1994 Act came
items: Art 243N (part of the 73rd Amendment) said that any state panchayat law that did not match the Amendment would stop working one year after the Amendment came into force (24 April 1993).
So AP had to pass a new, matching law: the AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994. This Art 243N rule is the correct reason for the 1994 Act.
Note: the 1986 mandal change and Nehru's 1959 inauguration at Shadnagar are both true facts, but one does not explain the other.

blocks.title: Early pattern: where the power sat
head: Aspect
Rajasthan–Andhra Pradesh pattern
Maharashtra–Gujarat pattern
rows: The block was the unit for planning and development
The district was the unit for planning and development

blocks.title: Other early facts (Laxmikanth)
items: The National Development Council (NDC) accepted the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee report in January 1958.
Rajasthan and AP adopted the three-tier system. Tamil Nadu adopted a two-tier system, and West Bengal a four-tier system.
Correct order: first the Mehta report was submitted (1957); then the NDC accepted it (January 1958); then Nagaur (2 October 1959); then Shadnagar (11 October 1959).

blocks.title: Unusual local bodies in some states (as in 1999) — old PYQ (previous year question)
head: Feature
State
rows: Zilla Parishads at the sub-divisional level

blocks.text: see Panchayati Raj: evolution and committees (national committees)

blocks.title: AP committee facts that could be checked
head: Committee or body
What is recorded
rows: Suggested that a revenue village with at least 1,000 people, or an annual income of Rs 2,000, should get its own separate gram panchayat. The government did not implement this.
Set up in the late 1960s, with the District Collector as chairman. They were abolished in 1970.

blocks.title: Gram Panchayat basics
head: Point
Fact
rows: Every gram panchayat is a body corporate (a legal person: it can own property, sue and be sued).
Minimum 5, maximum 21, including the sarpanch. The number depends on the village population at the last census (Section 7).
The village is divided into as many wards as there are member seats, with one seat in each ward (Section 10).
Ward members are elected on a NON-party basis (no party symbols).
One representative of each self-help group in the area is co-opted (added) to the gram panchayat. They can speak at meetings but CANNOT vote (Section 7(3)).
The MPTC member of the area (the elected member of the Mandal Parishad for that area) attends gram panchayat meetings. He can speak but cannot vote (Section 7(2)).
A member who stays away from all meetings for 90 days in a row loses membership (Section 20). He can apply for restoration within 30 days (Section 21).

The Panchayat Secretary convenes gram panchayat meetings, so that at least one meeting is held every month. If the sarpanch does not approve a meeting, the Secretary can convene it himself (Section 31).

blocks.title: Gram Sabha (all voters of the village)
head: Point
Fact
rows: Every person on the village electoral roll (voters' list).
At least twice a year (Section 6). The AP government fixed the dates as 14 April and 3 October.
Once every two months, that is, six times a year (Telangana Panchayat Raj Act, 2018, Section 6).
The sarpanch must call one if 50 voters or 10% of the voters, whichever is more, ask for it in writing.
The sarpanch (the upa-sarpanch in his absence).

The gram panchayat must place before it: the accounts and audit report, the administration report, the yearly works programme, proposals for new or higher taxes, and the selection of schemes, beneficiaries and locations.
Electing the upa-sarpanch. The members of the gram panchayat do that (Section 14).

Old Section 20A (added 2002): a sarpanch who did not hold the Gram Sabha meetings lost office. Act 1 of 2021 omitted (removed) Section 20A from 20 February 2020 and added Section 249B. Now, under Section 249B, a sarpanch who fails to convene the Gram Sabha meetings is 'deemed removed' (treated as removed) and cannot be re-elected for six years.

blocks.title: Functions of a gram panchayat
head: Aspect
Compulsory (must do)
Discretionary (may do)
rows: Street lighting (lighting of public roads and places); registration of births and deaths (Section 45)
Libraries and reading rooms; public slaughterhouses (Section 46)

blocks.title: Money of gram panchayats
items: Section 60: every gram panchayat must levy house tax (property tax) and a tax on village produce sold in the village (kolagaram).
2025 amendment to Section 60 (Bill introduced on 23 September 2025): gram panchayats can collect a fee when agricultural land is converted to non-agricultural use.
Surcharge on stamp duty (Section 69) is shared among gram panchayat, Mandal Parishad and Zilla Parishad in the ratio 3 : 1 : 1 (Government Order 226 of 2013).
Seigniorage (royalty on minor minerals such as sand and stone) is shared among gram panchayat, Mandal Parishad and Zilla Parishad in the ratio 25 : 50 : 25.
Entertainment tax share is divided between gram panchayat and Mandal Parishad in the ratio 60 : 40.

blocks.title: Sarpanch
head: Point
Fact
rows: Directly elected by the village voters, on a NON-party basis (no party symbols).

NOT by a no-confidence motion of ward members — the no-confidence section (Section 245) does not cover the sarpanch. The District Collector can remove a sarpanch for disobeying government orders, abuse of power, misconduct, misuse of panchayat funds or repeated failure in duties, after hearing his explanation (Section 249B, added in 2021). A removed sarpanch cannot be re-elected for six years.
Must be filled by a fresh election within 120 days (about four months) (Section 14(4)).
He does NOT approve the Mandal Parishad budget. The Zilla Parishad approves it (Section 192).

blocks.title: Upa-sarpanch (deputy sarpanch)
head: Point
Fact
rows: Elected by the gram panchayat members from among themselves; the sarpanch is also a member with a vote (Section 14(7)). The meeting is held on the day the election results are published.
Notice signed by at least half of the total members; it cannot be moved within four years of taking office; it passes with two-thirds of the total members (Section 245).
Cannot be moved within the first two years of taking office (Telangana Panchayat Raj Act, 2018, Section 30).

blocks.title: Panchayat Secretary
head: Point
Fact
rows: Appointed by the government (Section 30) — NOT elected by the gram panchayat.
Issues notice and convenes gram panchayat meetings (Section 31).

blocks.title: Two-child rule
items: From 1994, a person with more than two children could not contest local body elections in AP (Section 19(3)).
On 18 November 2024, the AP Assembly passed bills removing this rule from the Panchayat Raj law and the municipal laws. So such a person can now contest panchayat and municipal elections.
The rule came from state law, not from the 73rd Amendment. That is why a state can remove it by amending its own law.

blocks.title: Mandal Parishad
head: Point
Fact
rows: Under the 1986 Act, the voters directly elected the Mandal Praja Parishad president and the Zilla Praja Parishad chairman.
Directly elected on a party basis. Each MPTC area has a population of about 3,000 to 4,000 (Section 150) — not 10,000.
Ex-officio members (members because of another post)

The MLA (Member of the Legislative Assembly), the MLC (Member of the Legislative Council) and the Lok Sabha MP of the area, and a Rajya Sabha member who is a voter in the mandal (Section 149). They cannot vote in the election of the Mandal Parishad president, because only the elected MPTC members elect him (Section 153).
One person from a minority community (Section 149).

The District Collector; the sarpanches of the mandal; the ZPTC member of the mandal (its elected member in the Zilla Parishad); the Zilla Parishad chairperson; the Agricultural Market Committee president (Section 158). The District Central Cooperative Bank president is NOT in this list.
Elected by the MPTC members by show of hands, on a party basis (the party whip applies) (Section 153).

Notice signed by at least 50% of members, given to the Revenue Divisional Officer (RDO) or Sub-Collector, at least 15 days before the meeting. It cannot be moved within four years and needs two-thirds of the total members to pass.

Chief executive of the Mandal Parishad; appointed and paid by the state government (Section 167). He prepares the budget; the Mandal Parishad passes it and the Zilla Parishad then approves it. He is an officer, not a member.

blocks.title: Revenue mandal vs mandal parishad
items: Revenue mandals (the units for land revenue work) are more in number than mandal parishads.
Reason: urban areas have revenue mandals but may not have mandal parishads, because panchayat bodies are only for rural areas.

sections.heading: Zilla Praja Parishad and district bodies

blocks.title: Zilla Parishad (ZP)
head: Point
Fact
rows: One for each mandal (Section 178); directly elected on a party basis for five years.
Two persons from minority communities (Section 177). Only the elected members choose the chairman (Section 181), so the co-opted members do not vote in that election.
Permanent invitee to Zilla Parishad meetings, WITHOUT a vote (Section 188). He can also take part in standing committee meetings, but cannot vote.
The Zilla Parishad must meet at least once every 90 days. If the chairman fails, he loses office 30 days after that and cannot be elected chairman again for one year (Section 193(6)).
Appointed by the state government; holds the executive power of the Zilla Parishad (Section 186).
The Zilla Parishad approves the annual budgets of the Mandal Parishads (Section 192).

blocks.title: Removing a Zilla Parishad chairman by no-confidence (Section 245)

steps.detail: Signed by at least half of the total members. It cannot be given within four years of the chairman taking office.

steps.step: 2. Motion carried by two-thirds of the total members
3. The government removes the chairman; the vacancy is filled as a casual vacancy

blocks.title: Seven standing committees of every ZP (Section 187)
head: Committee
Note
rows: Chaired by the Zilla Parishad vice-chairman
blocks.note: Two other committees are chaired by women members nominated by the chairman; the chairman chairs the remaining four. There is NO 'Law and Order' committee — police is a state subject.

blocks.title: Who presides over which body
head: Body
Presiding officer
rows: A State Minister nominated by the government, as ex-officio chairperson (NOT the Collector, NOT the Zilla Parishad chairman)

blocks.title: District Planning Committee
items: Provided by Art 243ZD (Part IXA, added by the 74th Amendment).
Not less than four-fifths of its members are elected from among the members of the panchayats and municipalities in the district.

In AP (District Planning Committees Act, 2004), a State Minister nominated by the government is the chairperson. The Zilla Parishad chairman attends as a permanent special invitee if he is not already an elected member.

blocks.title: New districts and ZPs (as of Nov 2026)
items: 4 April 2022: AP's 13 districts were reorganised into 26.
27 November 2025: Polavaram and Markapuram districts were formed — AP now has 28 districts.
September 2026 (Government Order 114): the 13 Zilla Praja Parishads are to be reorganised into 28, one for each district, after the old bodies' term ended (24 September 2026).

sections.heading: State Election Commission, Finance Commission and 2026 polls

blocks.title: AP State Election Commission
head: Point
Fact
rows: Art 243K. Panchayat elections are conducted by the State Election Commission. It issues the notification and allots symbols — not the Election Commission of India, not the Chief Electoral Officer, and not the Collector.
17 June 1994, under the AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994.
Residuary AP (the AP left after the 2014 division)
The Governor constituted a separate commission on 30 January 2016.
Single-member commission, appointed by the Governor on the state government's recommendation; term five years.
Must hold or have held a post not below Principal Secretary to the Government (Section 200).
Can be removed only in the same way, and on the same grounds, as a High Court judge (Section 200).
An ordinance (a temporary law made by the Governor) tried to cut the commissioner's term to three years; the AP High Court struck it down.

blocks.title: State Election Commissioners to remember
head: Person
Post
rows: AP State Election Commissioner from April 2016
AP State Election Commissioner from April 2021
AP State Election Commissioner from 21 April 2026
First Telangana State Election Commissioner (2015 to April 2020)

blocks.title: State Finance Commission
items: Art 243I: the Governor sets up a State Finance Commission every five years to review panchayat finances.

Section 235 of the AP Act required the first AP State Finance Commission within one year of the 73rd Amendment coming into force (24 April 1993), that is, by 1994, and a new one every five years after that.
Art 280(3)(bb): the Union Finance Commission recommends funds to be added to a state's Consolidated Fund for its panchayats, based on that state's Finance Commission recommendations.

blocks.title: AP local bodies in 2026 (as of Nov 2026)

items.what: Dedicated Commission on BC (Backward Classes) reservation set up (Government Order Ms No. 3)
items.detail: Single member: Rajiv Ranjan Mishra (retired IAS officer). It was needed to meet the Supreme Court's 'triple test' (K. Krishna Murthy and Vikas Kishanrao Gawali cases): (1) a dedicated commission makes a current study of backwardness; (2) reservation is fixed for each local body on its advice; (3) total reservation stays within 50%.

items.what: Terms of the sarpanches ended before new polls; special officers took charge from 3 April
items.detail: Art 243E: a panchayat's term is five years, and elections must be completed before the term ends.

items.what: State Election Commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha (in office from 21 April 2026) announced the schedule
MPTC and ZPTC polling (revised from 3 November); counting from 7 November
items.detail: The NDA alliance (Telugu Desam Party, Jana Sena and Bharatiya Janata Party) won most seats.

items.what: Gram panchayat (sarpanch and ward) polls in three phases — scheduled (one report gives 3 December for the third phase)

items: AP was SECOND, not first: Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959), then AP (Shadnagar, 11 October 1959).
The AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 came into force on 30 May 1994; the mandal parishads came into effect on 15 January 1987.
Sarpanch and ward members: NON-party elections. MPTC and ZPTC members: party basis.
A sarpanch cannot be removed by no-confidence; the Collector removes him (Section 249B). No-confidence applies to the upa-sarpanch, the Mandal Parishad president and the Zilla Parishad chairman.
A removed sarpanch is barred for SIX years (Section 249B, 2021); a removed Mandal Parishad president or Zilla Parishad chairman is barred for two years (Section 249(3)).
The Panchayat Secretary convenes gram panchayat meetings; he is appointed, not elected.
Self-help group representatives in a gram panchayat and the Collector in a Zilla Parishad have NO vote.
The AP District Planning Committee is chaired by a State Minister — not the Collector and not the Zilla Parishad chairman.
The two-child rule was a state rule (removed in November 2024), not part of the 73rd Amendment.

items.what: Charter issued to set up the Madras Municipal Corporation

items.what: Madras Municipal Corporation comes into existence — the first municipal corporation in India

items.what: Municipal corporations set up in Bombay and Calcutta

items.what: Lord Mayo's Resolution on financial decentralisation

items.what: Lord Ripon's Resolution on local self-government
items.detail: Called the 'Magna Carta' (great charter) of local self-government. Ripon is called the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India'.

items.what: 'Local Government' is in the State List (Seventh Schedule)
items.detail: It is NOT in the Concurrent List.

Bill
What happened

Not passed; it lapsed (ended) when the Lok Sabha was dissolved

blocks.title: Key dates of the 74th Amendment Act
head: Step
Date

items: Audit (Art 243Z): the state legislature, by law, provides for maintenance of municipal accounts and their audit (not the Governor).

Courts (Art 243ZG): a law on delimitation of constituencies or allotment of seats cannot be questioned in any court. A municipal election can be challenged only by an election petition before an authority set by state law. rows: Grants were split into two parts: a basic grant (given to every body) and a performance grant (given only if the body meets set conditions). Gram panchayats: 90% basic and 10% performance. Municipalities: 80% basic and 20% performance.
